sp.p: This pithy notice from my good ally of France, can mean no less than that my brother Richard hath escap'd from Austria's prison; he hath well describ'd my brother's character, and my peril,
‘Shift for yourself, the devil has broke loose.” I hear too, Cedric and his Saxon followers, aided by Locksley and his outlaws, dare to besiege the castle of my friend.
How now, what means this? are the Saxons in rebellion? where is Frondebœuf?

sp.speaker: Sir B.
sp.p: Frondebœuf has found a grave among the blazing rafters of his castle, nor is this news the worst; King Richard is return'd: nay, start not, 'tis true as truth; all's lost with you and us, and if once he heads an army—why looks my prince thus earnestly?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: There is grave cause; come hither, valiant knight. I have long time been thinking on this chance, nothing like forecast;—knowest thou, Sir Brian, how he journeys?

sp.speaker: Sir B.
sp.p: Alone, quite unattended.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: There's but one road he can journey to our safety. Mark me, he must be met.—

sp.speaker: Sir B.
sp.p: Be met! but not by me; I was his prisoner once, he gave me freedom, I will not harm a feather in his crest—

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Who spoke of harming him? think'st thou, sir knave, I meant he should be slain? a prison would be better, no matter whether in Austria or Britain. Our uncle Robert liv'd in Cardiff Castle.

sp.speaker: Sir B.
sp.p: And died there—in the opinion of some great men, there is no prison-builder like your sexton, no dungeon like a church-vault; but prison, or tomb, I wash my hands of it.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Villain! would'st thou betray our council?

sp.speaker: Sir B.
sp.p: I am no betrayer, nor must the name of villain couple with mine.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: But thy free followers draw few such nice distinctions.

sp.speaker: Sir. B.
sp.p: My lord, my lord, you have sufficient ruffians of your own; not one of mine shall budge on such an errand. Prince, I will abide by thee in all becomes a knight, but never, never, will I turn assassin.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: My father, King Henry, had faithful servants, and had but to say he was plagued by a factious priest, when straight the blood of Becket stain'd the marble of his own altar: Fitzurse must be the man; I have promised to make him chancellor, and while he thinks of that, his arm will stick at nought. Well, let him think! A chancellor indeed! my brother's murderer will hardly be the man to keep my conscience.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: A Garden at a Preceptory House of the Templars, at Templestowe. The Grand Master, Lucas de Beaumanoir enters, followed by Malvoisin.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Valiant brother of our order, what avails it that I, Lucas de Beaumanoir, Grand Master of the Templars, shou'd visit this your country to discover how shamefully our statutes are disgraced?— Is it not true that the head of the preceptory of Templestowe, even Sir Brian, has brought hither a paramour, who is now concealed within his walls?

sp.speaker: De M.
sp.p: 'Tis but too true that the irregularities of our English Templars, are, if possible, as bad or worse than yours in France.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: But I will use my power to cleanse this Augean stable.
Now, brother, thou hast leave to say—what with thee?

sp.speaker: Dam.
sp.p: A Jew, noble and reverend father, prays to deliver a letter to brother Sir Brian de Bois Guilbert.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Let him bring it here, and let a guard attend our call; it may be wanted.

sp.speaker: Dam.
sp.p: The Jew is here, so please you.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Now, sirrah, thy business with Sir Brian?

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: I bear to him a letter, please your reverend valour, from holy prior Aymer.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Oh evil times! said I not so? and, lo, a Cistercian Friar sends a letter to a soldier of the Temple, and can find no better carrier than a Jew! —it cannot be.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: 'Tis here, so please you.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Back—I touch not misbelievers but with the sword—take thou the letter, brother,
and give it me.

sp.speaker: De Ma.
sp.p: And wilt thou break the seal?—

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: And shall I not? Our order gives me power—here, here's goodly stuff for a priest to write to a preceptor

“We rejoice thou hast escaped with that fair Jewish sorceress, whose black eyes have bewitch'd thee; yet beware this second witch of Endor come not to the knowledge of thy Grand Master, who careth not for black eyes or cherry cheeks, and is come from Normandy to diminish your mirth, and amend your misdoings: therefore give her up to her father, the Jew, who will pay roundly for her ransom. 'Till our next merry meeting o'er the wine cup, fare thee well.” Here's order and regularity! and who is this “second witch of Endor?”

sp.speaker: De Ma.
sp.p: A pupil of Miriam of York, who was burnt for sorcery, and of whom she learned the art of healing, as some in this house can testify. She lately undertook to cure a knight, who—

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Silence!—is it true she hath recovered those in danger?

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: Many, when other human aid was vain; but the blessing of Jacob's father was upon her.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Did she use cabalistic words?

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: A balsam only of marvellous virtue, which she had of a sage matron of our race of—of Miriam.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Aye, of a wicked sorceress like herself— a witch, whose ashes were scatter'd to the four winds, and so be it to me and to mine order if her pupil do not share her fate. Damien, spurn hence this Hebrew from our gate—shoot him if he oppose or turn again— with his daughter we will deal as our high office warrants.

div.stage: [Exit with Conrad, Isaac stands as if petrified.

sp.speaker: Damien.
sp.p: Come, old man, thou hast heard what I am commanded—I am sorry for thee, but dare not say it loud—I feel for thee, but must not appear to do so. Our duties here are too strict, to permit any gratifying indulgence. Art thou awake—dost thou not hear me, Jew?

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: Child of my affliction, why shou'd thy threaten'd death bring my grey hairs with sorrow to the grave— Is she not here? May I not see her, Christian?

sp.speaker: Dam.
sp.p: Impossible!—not now at least; come! courage! she yet liveth.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: Aye, liveth as Daniel in the lions' den, captive to men of Belial, who will wreak their cruelty, sparing neither her youth, nor her comely favor. Oh! she was a crown of palm to my grey locks, and she must wither in a night like the Gourd of Jonah.

sp.speaker: Dam.
sp.p: She is not yet condemn'd—

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Nay, let me, let me see him.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: 'Tis she! 'tis she! oh take this jewel, take it—
What! a Christian, and refuse!
Ah! my child!

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: My stubborn guard, who would'nt bend to pity, listen'd to golden argument; and oh! for the last time it is permitted, perhaps, that I embrace my father.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: For the last time! oh Rebecca, daughter of Rachael, child of my old age, the darkness of the shadow of death hath encompass'd thee, and in its depth shall thy father also fall.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Nay! nay! but thou may'st yet save thyself and me, should I be condemned for this imaginary crime; the custom of these people will allow a champion in my cause.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: And who will dare espouse an outcast's cause? the daughter of a Jew? whose only faults are truth to her religion, duty to her unhappy father, and having reliev'd the miseries of her fellow creatures without staying to enquire whether they were Jew or Christian.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Yes, there is one—I think—I know not—but I hope it, who will come forward even in my cause— Wilfred, the son of Cedric whom these Gentiles call Ivanhoe, if he can yet endure the weight of his armour; at least send to him, father, and say that I am innocent, he hath favour among the strong men of his people, he was our companion in the house of bondage, and may at least find some one to do battle in his stead, shou'd he be still unable.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: I go—but shou'd I fail, and shou'dst thou die!

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: I shall die free of the guilt I am charg'd withal, and do not thou afterwards tarry in this place of bloodshed, betake thee to the Saracen land where thy brother dwelleth.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: It shall be so; farewel, my daughter, my daughter, offspring of my love! yes, if all faileth—I will leave this land, and seek the Saracen; for less bitter are the cruelties of the Moors unto the race of Jacob, than the tender Christian hospitalities of the Nazarines of England: fare thee well!

sp.speaker: Dam.
sp.p: Now, Hebrew; I must conduct thee hence.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: Templar, altho' thou wilt not take my gold, be kind to her if thou cans't, be kind to my Rebecca, thou weep'st, can it be possible? a Templar weep, what cause hast thou?

sp.speaker: Dam.
sp.p: I have a daughter, but 'twere treason here to name it.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: True nature is banish'd here—thou hast a daughter? may she never know the peril of my Rebecca, or her good father half the woes of Isaac.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: My guards return not—ah, who comes? the cause of all my trouble.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: Tell not me—he dare not—Rebecca is the victim of my folly, not the cause, nor shall even Beaumanoir, this mighty Master, flush'd with power, punish the innocent.

sp.speaker: De Mal.
sp.p: This rage avails not, you are pitied as the victim of magical delusion, and she as a sorceress will be doom'd to suffer.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: She shall not, by heaven!

sp.speaker: De Mal.
sp.p: Nor you, nor any one that lives, can save her, but the Grand Master; go throw yourself at his feet.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: Not at his feet—no, rather to his very beard I'll say—

sp.speaker: De Mal.
sp.p: That you love this Jewess to distraction, and for her sake will relinquish the chance of becoming Grand Master yourself, for the pleasure of breaking a mercenary spear abroad, but I must leave you to prepare the judgment-seat.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: So soon?

sp.speaker: De Mal.
sp.p: Directly, and see the cause of all this trouble, take thy farewel, for I must send a guard to lead her to the hall—bethink thee—be a man.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: Be a man, then shou'd I act in stern defiance of this churlish order. Be a man! oh, who is a man who can desert a woman? yet tho' I wou'd not abandon her to fate, shou'd I be again repulsed, my vengeance would be equal to my love—Rebecca!

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: What wou'dst thou say? speak briefly, if thou meanest ought but to witness the misery thou hast caused, let me know it—and then so please you, leave me to myself, my pre-judged trial tells me, the step between this world and a better will be short and terrible, and I shall have but a few minutes to prepare for it.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: There is indeed a way from all this trouble, listen but to the suit I made ere while.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: If thou art a man—be one—if a Christian, shew that mercy which rather your tongues than your actions pretend to, and save me from a dreadful death without seeking a requital which wou'd change thy magnanimity into the basest barter.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: Aye! if thou'lt go with me far from this England to Palestine, where no Templar's scruples fetter us; rather with Saladin we'll league ourselves than endure the scorn of bigots we contemn; there shalt thou, without the forms of wedlock, be a queen, a free unfettered queen.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Now, God be gracious to me, for the succour of man is hopeless!—leave me.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: And wou'dst thou, sooner than requite the love of a Norman noble, die the death of the worst of criminals, consum'd on a blazing pile? dispersed to the elements, not a relict left of that graceful form? Rebecca, 'tis not in woman to sustain this project; thou must yield to my suit.

div.stage: (A guard enters and signs to Rebecca.)

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Thou art mistaken, yet I forgive thee, tho' thou'rt the author of my early death. Thy Norman nobility is poor compared with her's, descended from princes of Judah—now no more! Yet, though trampled down like the shorn grass, I will not shame such high descent—I envy not thy blood-won honors, I envy not thy Norman ancestry, nor yet thy faith, which still is in thy mouth, but never in thy practice, Fare thee well.

div.stage: (Drum rolls as she is taken off.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: There is a spell upon me—what's to be done?—I must attend and try at least to save her, and yet her obstinacy—Oh! speak the truth! In man, 'twou'd be called courage—nobleness—there is a lurking fiend which tells me here young Ivanhoe is the curs'd bar to what I wish—if so—oh! no—I'll save her, be it possible—but not for him—oh! no, no, not for him!

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: The grand Hall of the Templars—The Grand Master, Preceptors, Knights, and Brethren, arranged in order of judgment, as for a trial.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: You've heard the cause of our assembly; bring forth the accused—
We have heard, Rebecca, of thy crimes: besides alluring from his duty a champion of our order, it will be prov'd thy sorceries surpass all we of late have read of—call the witnesses.

sp.speaker: Gur.
sp.p: I am one; while journeying for my liege lord, I was way laid and nearly slain by free knights followers, good Christian men, but skilful in hard blows; the prisoner heard of it, and sent me balms, medicine, and money, which, together, joined like magic to set me on my legs—I am now a free man, yet wou'd I give up more than my life, even my new-gain'd liberty, and be your slave, so you wou'd set her free.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: She used some words?

sp.speaker: Gur.
sp.p: Not one—'twas sent to me by a strange hand, nor did I know she was my benefactress till to-day— then hasten'd hither to attest the truth.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Some talismanic characters accompanied the drugs she sent?

sp.speaker: Gur.
sp.p: Some call'd 'em Hebrew, but whate'er they were, I've cause to bless them.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Fellow, get thee hence; nor dare speak in favour of a sorceress—what other charges have ye?

sp.speaker: De Mal.
sp.p: Twenty at least, whom she has rais'd from beds of hopeless sickness, nine physicians have sworn the cures she effected were impossible, unless by downright witchery.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Enough, enough—speak, what hast thou to say?

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: My life is wreckless, but I will not cast away the gift of heaven. The imaginary crime of sorcery I deny—I maintain my innocence, and declare the falsehood of the accusation—I challenge privilege of trial by combat, and will appear by my champion.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: And who will lay lance in rest for a sorceress—who will be champion for an infidel?

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Heaven will raise me up a champion; it cannot be said, that in merry England, the hospitable, the generous, the free, where so many lose their lives for honour, there shall not be found one to fight for justice: there lies my gage.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Give me the glove, a slight and frail gage for so dread a purpose—see'st thou, maid, as this small glove of thine is to one of our heavier gaunt lets, so is thy cause to that of the holy order thou defiest.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Cast Innocence into the scale, and the glove of silk outweighs the glove of iron.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: One offer will I make; renounce thine errors, and thou art free.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: I am unskill'd to argue for my faith, but I can die for it

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: To whom shall we deliver this to be our champion?

sp.speaker: De Mal.
sp.p: It must be our head preceptor, Brian de Bois Guilbert.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: It is but justice—shou'd he refuse, his honour and his life are forfeit both.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Is any here, who for the love of a good cause, or ample hire, will do the errand of a distress'd being? no one? And in English land shall I then want that charity, which wou'd not be refused the worst of criminals.

sp.speaker: Gur.
sp.p: Write thy message, damsel, and I am thy man—
A neighbour here says, none but a fool will take it—now I, like my fellow-servant, Wamba, have been a fool all my life, and am willing, like the fair Jewess, to die in my profession.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Bear our command, with this glove, to Sir Brian—remove the prisoner and close the court.

div.stage: (Muffled drums—Rebecca gives a paper to Gurth, who goes off with it. She is guarded off on one side—the Grand Master descends and is going off, on the other, when the scene closes.)

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Enter the Black Knight and Wamba.

sp.speaker: B. Kni.
sp.p: Fool, thou wast given me by thy master, Cedric, to be a guide, can'st tell me why?

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: No, courteous sir, unless it was because he thought valour and folly often go together.

sp.speaker: B. Kni.
sp.p: Did he not also think thou knewest the way?

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: Aye, sir, and more than that, I know there is a horn to sound three notes, if we shou'd be in danger.

sp.speaker: B. Kni.
sp.p: We are in no danger of wanting it, nor shall I sound it—come fool—what wou'dst thou?

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: I wou'd borrow it so please you—for when valour and folly travel, folly shou'd bear the horn, because she blows it best—and it will be needful too, for an I mistake not, there are company in yonder brake, on the look out for us.

sp.speaker: B. Kni.
sp.p: By St. George thy guess is near the mark.

div.stage: (An arrow glances on the Black Knight's breast-plate.)
(Music. Fitzurse and Ruffians attack the Black Knight, who beats them back, and they stand at bay.)

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: Hold! hold! a parley.

sp.speaker: B. Kni.
sp.p: Dos't fear to draw thy sword, fool?

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: This is my sword, and I always prefer music before fighting—
Now, gentlemen, a fair field and no favor.

div.stage: (Draws and joins in the fray—the Black Knight is nearly beaten down—Wamba blows again, the wood seems peopled with Yeomen—Lockley's at their head —Ivanhoe rushes between the Black Knight and Fitzurse, and strikes the latter to the ground—the helmet of the Black Knight is beaten off, when Locksley and his men rush forward to the rescue—the Ruffians are disarmed, kneel, and cry—Pardon! pardon!

sp.speaker: Ivan.
sp.p: Assassins! who shall grant it?

sp.speaker: B. Kni.
sp.p: Their king! Richard!
Ivanhoe, thou hast well kept my secret—Locksley, thou art a true subject—
Such implements as those are worthless of my anger; but there,
Wamba, remove the helmet of that loyal knight, that we may know our friends.

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: Come, valiant bush-fighter, hold up your head—a great man wants to speak to you—don't be modest.

sp.speaker: K. Rich.
sp.p: Fitzurse! disloyal friend, who urged thee to this deed?

sp.speaker: Fitz.
sp.p: Thy father's son—Prince John.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Add too, thine own ambition and revenge, I wrong'd thee not.

sp.speaker: Fitz.
sp.p: Thou didst disdain my daughter's hand— and—

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: And acted as I ought; thou do'st not ask thy life?

sp.speaker: Fitz.
sp.p: He that is in the lion's clutch knows it were needless.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Take it then unask'd, take thy life; leave England and never name my brother as connected with this villainy; break this condition, or breathe ought to attaint the honour of my house, and not the church itself shall be thy sanctuary; I'll hang thee out to feed the ravens, from the very pinnacle of thy Norman Castle—hence.
Locksley, give him a steed.

div.stage: Gurth enters and gives Ivanhoe a Letter.

sp.speaker: Lock.
sp.p: And but for my king, I'd send a shaft after the skulking villain, should spare him the labour of a journey. And now, my liege, my pardon may be needful—the pardon, not of Locksley, but of Robert of Huntingdon, or Robin Hood, with these his merry men.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: You have done good service—Rise, we throw a veil over all faults done in our absence—we were wrong to leave ye.

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: Aye! good my liege; for with all due reverence, when the cat's away the mice will play.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Fool, thou hast belied thy title, and shalt be rewarded too; but where's my faithful Wilfred, of Ivanhoe? what news hast thou to steal thy color thus?

sp.speaker: Iva.
sp.p: From you my liege I dare not aught conceal. Rebecca is attainted of her life, on the poor plea of sorcery, and my fell foe, Sir Brian, is the champion this day against her.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: To horse then, merry men—I'll be her champion.

sp.speaker: Iva.
sp.p: Against a subject, sire? oh! no indeed! and Brian challenger! my poor sword half meets my hand already to oppose him.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Thou'rt yet too weak.

sp.speaker: Iva.
sp.p: In such a cause as this, dwarfs become giants.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Huntingdon, to horse.

sp.speaker: Lock.
sp.p: So please my liege to take some slight refreshment.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Be speedy then, there's work yet to be done. I meant not to be known 'till I had reach'd my capital, which now is here, and every where—while so surrounded, happy the monarch who can thus behold in every face a friend.

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: Gurth, we'll to court, I'm tired of these woods.

sp.speaker: Gur.
sp.p: So am not I—I'm free—free! good Wamba!

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: Not more than welcome, Gurth; well, when I grow great I'll come and see thee and thy herd of— of—what do you call those grunting things, that—

sp.speaker: Gur.
sp.p: Can'st thou forget thy friends, my merry swine —you courtiers have short memories.

sp.speaker: Wam.
sp.p: We have, and if I grow great at court, my comrades will soon forget I ever was a fool, unless I chance to lose my place; and if I do, I'll come and enjoy my little loaves and fishes next door to your free and independent piggery.

div.head: SCENE THE LAST.
div.stage: Tilt Yard of the Preceptory, and Solemn Procession to the lists—a Throne for the Grand Master—and a funeral Pile for Rebecca—Rebecca brought on last —She is seaed.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Where is the champion of our order?

sp.speaker: Sir B.
sp.p: Here,—if I may speak with the accused, bloodshed may be prevented and she be yet led to renounce her error.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Briefly then, and in presence.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: I have no portion in thee, cruel man, what wou'dst thou with me?

sp.speaker: Sir B.
sp.p: No champion will appear; seem but to yield to their entreaty, and the swiftest horse that ever knight bestrode, waits to convey us hence. Oh, see the dreadful preparations—see that pile!—do not refuse to save thy life and me!—in one short hour pursuit and enquiry shall be far behind —a new world of pleasure shall open to thee—and to me, a new career of fame.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Tempter, begone! surrounded thus by foes, I hold thee as my deadliest and worst, avoid me in the name of goodness.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: Relentless woman, in thine own despight I'll save thee!—shou'd any champion come, I'll deal with him; then, in the moment of their fiendlike exultation, bear her hence, or shou'd I fall, 'twill end the fearful struggle.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: No champion comes.
Make way there!

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Ah! shou'd it be! alas! my father?

div.stage: Enter Isaac, who runs towards his Daughter, and is prevented.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: It may not be! the hour for indulgence fast elapses; take hence the old man.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: Wou'd you tear a father from his dying child? Monsters! barbarians! Oh for thunder's power to—

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Father, be calm, we have a friend in heaven who yet will manifest—

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: Alas! too late!—My messengers have return'd no champion to be found, and all afraid to take the side of a poor friendless woman. Nay, let me go, or where my child must suffer, there shall be my grave, or my unburied bones shall whiten'd lay, a monument of Christian cruelty.

sp.speaker: Reb.
sp.p: Now! now! while he perceives it not—since no one dare appear in my behalf, lead me to yonder fatal pile, and consummate your duty.
sp.stage: (A trumpet heard and a shout—Rebecca falls on one knee.)
sp.p: Then there is yet a friend to innocence—

div.stage: (The trumpet sounds again, and Ivanhoe appears, faint and breathless.)

sp.speaker: Ivan.
sp.p: I have outstripp'd my sovereign, and must abide his generous anger. Now, where's the champion in this holy cause—Wilfred of Ivanhoe, the son of Cedric, defies him to the death.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: I will not fight with thee—get thy wounds heal'd.

sp.speaker: Ivan.
sp.p: My wounds are heal'd, and by the skill of her whose virtuous knowledge you have dared term sorcery. Nay, jealous knight, 'tis not the cause of love, but honest gratitude, which brings me here—my sword is ready in a righteous cause, nor shall she perish while this hand can wield it. Rebecca's champion boldly then defies, and calls each false accuser of a helpless maid—aye, and the knight who can support them—cowards!

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: Sound trumpets, sound—and, should I conquer, grant me one poor request—'tis written here—

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: If it not give offence to—

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: If, or not, promise, or I will throw my weapon down, and stain your order with a coward's name.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: 'Tis granted with reservation—

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: No reservation! swear!
sp.stage: (Sir Brian to Ivanhoe over a cross as if taking a solemn vow.)
sp.p: My hate to thee and thine to me may now be satisfied.

sp.speaker: Ivan.
sp.p: This be my answer to thee.

div.stage: (Trumpets—they fight—just as Sir Brian falls, a shout and cry is heard, and King Richard enters with all his party from the forest.)

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Hold! hold! I am too late, then—I had meant Sir Brian for my own sword. Was it well, Ivanhoe, to take on thee this maiden's safety and thine own, when thou could'st scarcely keep thy saddle here?

sp.speaker: Ivan.
sp.p: 'Twere better I had died than you had risk'd your sacred person.

sp.speaker: Sir Bri.
sp.p: Boast not thy conquest, youth—I meant it for thee—peruse that paper when I am no more— Those knights have sworn to grant what e'er it asks, and when 'tis read, e'en you, Rebecca, will forgive— and you, my injured master, pardon! pardon!

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Thou hast sav'd the damsel: ere we yet release her—

sp.speaker: Ivan.
sp.p: Ere ye release her—have ye a shade of right, or if ye had, did ye not swear to grant what this requests —

—“Should I conquer, I demand by your oath the safety of Rebecca; should I fall, persecute no longer her father nor herself—so may you atone for the injury they've met from Brian”— And now ye suffering pair—

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Hold thee, bold knight—we must deliberate, ere yet this paper. How now, what would'st thou—

sp.speaker: Attend.
sp.p: I wou'd advise thee to depart this realm. Philip de Malvoisin, I arrest thee of high treason.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: Arrest—who dares?

sp.speaker: Attend.
sp.p: I, Humphrey Bohun, Earl of Essex, Lord Constable of England.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: By whose command?

sp.speaker: Attend.
sp.p: My sovereign's! Richard, lawful King of England.

sp.speaker: G. Mas.
sp.p: A dreadful punishment will wait this boldness.

sp.speaker: Ivan.
sp.p: Proud priest, my king disdains an answer to thee. His royal standard floats above thy temple mummery, nor all thy threats can pull that daring ensign, from where a British hand with justice plants it—Beware, thou'rt in the lion's grasp.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Templars, go where ye list, but rule not here. Come, Ivanhoe, thy destin'd bride, Rowena, and thy father's favor, await to crown thy gallant loyalty.

sp.speaker: Isa.
sp.p: And dare such humble subjects, as my dear Rebecca and myself intrude—with heartfelt gratitude to you, and you, and all, we'd say—our minds, our hearts, and means shall ever be devoted to our country and the good king we have so long revered.
